---
# The Uses of Disorientation

It begins with a small, specific humiliation: you emerge from a subway station into a city you thought you knew, and nothing resolves. The building that should be to your left is not there. The street runs the wrong way. For perhaps four seconds you are genuinely, usefully lost — and then the phone comes out, the blue dot appears, the little arrow swivels obediently to the north, and the world snaps back into legibility like a bone going back into its socket. The relief is real. And so, though you don't notice it, is the loss.

We have spent a great deal of human history trying to solve the problem of not knowing where we are, and we have largely solved it. This is a triumph, and I don't want to be the sort of person who complains about triumphs. Emergency services find people in the wilderness now. No one dies of a wrong turn in a strange city the way they used to. But it is worth asking what we traded, because the trade was not nothing. The capacity to be lost is a capacity, and like most capacities it can atrophy from disuse. When it goes, something goes with it — not just a skill but a whole mode of attention, a way of being in a place that is older than maps and considerably older than us.

To understand what we're losing, it helps to understand what the brain is actually doing when it knows where it is. In 1971, a young neuroscientist named John O'Keefe, working in a cramped lab at University College London, was recording from single neurons in the hippocampus of a rat as it moved around a small arena. Most cells fired in a noisy, undifferentiated way. But a few fired only when the rat was in one particular spot — a specific corner, a specific patch of floor — and stayed silent everywhere else. O'Keefe called them *place cells*, and the name was almost too plain for what they implied: that the brain contains, as a literal physical fact, a map. Each cell is a coordinate. A rat with a few thousand of them can know, in some rudimentary way, where it is in the world.

It took another three decades to find the rest of the machinery. In the early 2000s, May-Britt and Edvard Moser, working in Trondheim, discovered neurons in a neighboring region that fire in a hexagonal lattice, like the work of a very tidy surveyor — *grid cells*, they called them, a coordinate system overlaid on the map. Other researchers found *head-direction cells*, which track which way you're facing, and *border cells*, which mark the edges of things. By 2014 the Nobel Committee had given all three a prize, and the citation was almost poetic: the scientists had discovered "a positioning system, an inner GPS, in the brain." It was a beautiful finding, and also an ironic one, because at almost exactly the moment we learned that the brain contains a GPS, we began outsourcing that GPS to a machine — and the machine's version turns out to be a much thinner thing than the one we were born with.

The first hint came from taxi drivers. In 2000, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues at UCL scanned the brains of London cabbies, a population famous for "the Knowledge" — the grueling, years-long memorization of some 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross, a test so hard that it reportedly shrinks the pool of applicants more reliably than any other qualification in Britain. Maguire found that the posterior hippocampus of the cabbies was significantly larger than in control subjects, and larger still in those who had been driving longest. The brain, it seemed, had grown a muscle for navigation. But the finding had a shadow: the anterior hippocampus was slightly *smaller*, suggesting a kind of trade — an allocation of tissue toward spatial memory at the expense of something else. More recent work has complicated the picture, but the broad lesson has held up. The brain allocates resources to what it does. A place you have learned is physically inscribed; a place you have merely visited is not.

Then came the studies of what happens when the machine does the work. In 2020, a team led by Louisa Dahmani and Véronique Bohbot at McGill looked at a group of adults and asked a simple question: how often do you use GPS? They then had them navigate a virtual environment. The heavy GPS users performed worse. Their brains, on imaging, showed less activity in the hippocampus and more in the caudate nucleus — a region associated with habit and stimulus-response learning, the "turn left at the gas station" circuitry rather than the "I know where I am" circuitry. The researchers were careful, as good scientists are, to note that the direction of causation is not settled. Maybe GPS use erodes spatial memory. Maybe people with weak spatial memory gravitate to GPS. Probably both are true, in a feedback loop that runs quietly and mostly in one direction.

I am not, let me be clear, arguing against maps. Maps are one of the great human achievements, and we should not romanticize the era before them, which was full of people dying in ditches. But there is a distinction worth preserving between *using* a map and *outsourcing* navigation to one. The Polynesians used maps of a kind — but their maps were in their heads and bodies, encoded in chants and star paths and the feel of a swell against the hull. To sail from Tahiti to Hawaii without instruments, as navigators did for centuries, you had to hold an entire ocean in your mind: the rising and setting of specific stars, the way the swells refract around islands you cannot see, the flight paths of birds at dawn, the color of clouds over lagoons. It was a form of attention so complete that the navigator was, in a sense, indistinguishable from the route. When Mau Piailug, a navigator from Satawal in Micronesia, guided the Hōkūleʻa from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 using only these methods, he did something that the modern world had largely forgotten was possible. The voyage is often told as a story about cultural revival. It is also a story about what a human being can know.

Being lost is what that knowledge is *for*. The navigator is never lost, but the navigator is always, in a sense, in danger of being lost — always running a model of the world that could be wrong, and checking it against the water. That constant low-grade uncertainty is the engine of attention. When the model might be wrong, you look. When the phone can't be wrong, you don't. The blue dot is never mistaken, and so the world around it becomes wallpaper. This is the real cost: not the loss of a skill, but the loss of a reason to look.

Consider what happens when you look. The psychologist Eleanor Gibson coined a term, *affordances*, for the qualities of an environment that suggest what you can do with it: a chair affords sitting, a low wall affords perching, a path affords walking. When you navigate by your own wits, the world becomes a dense field of affordances. That alley might cut through; that hill might give a view; that smell of bread means a bakery, which means a street, which means the river is that way, because bakeries cluster where the water was. You are reading the city like a text in a language you half-know, and the reading is the pleasure. When you navigate by blue dot, the world becomes an undifferentiated surface through which you are being conveyed. The affordances don't disappear, but you don't see them, because you have no reason to. The city stops being a place and becomes a corridor.

There is a name for the opposite disposition, and it comes from nineteenth-century Paris. The *flâneur* was Baudelaire's invention — the idler who walks the city without purpose, observing, absorbing, letting the streets dictate the route. Walter Benjamin made the flâneur a central figure of his unfinished arcades project, seeing in him a kind of proto-modern consciousness: someone for whom the city was not a problem to be solved but a text to be read. The flâneur is the anti-navigator. He has nowhere to be, and so he can be anywhere. In the 1950s, the Situationists took this idea and made it a method. Guy Debord's "Theory of the Dérive" proposed a deliberate practice of drifting through the city, letting the environment's "psychogeography" — its emotional contours, its currents of attraction and repulsion — pull you where it would. The point was to see the city as it actually is, rather than as the planners intended it to be seen. It was a technique for getting lost on purpose, and it was meant to be revelatory. It still is.

You don't need a theory to do it. You need only to walk out your door and turn the wrong way, deliberately, and then keep going, and then turn again for no reason, and then notice that after twenty minutes you are in a place you have passed a thousand times and never once seen. This happens to me with depressing regularity, and each time it feels like a small failure and a small gift. The city is bigger than my model of it. That is a good thing to be reminded of.

The informal geography of desire paths is a useful corrective here, because it shows that the map is never the territory, no matter how good the map. A desire path — also called a desire line — is the trail worn into the grass beside a paved walkway by people who have decided that the official route is wrong. Every campus has them. Every park. They are the physical record of a thousand small acts of navigation-by-wits, and they are always more efficient than the thing the planners built. Landscape architects have learned to study them, sometimes deliberately leaving the paving off a new quadrangle for a year to see where people walk, then paving *that*. It is a humbling concession: the map must follow the feet, not the other way round. The feet know things the map does not.

What the feet know is something like the difference between a route and a place. A route is a line. A place is a knot of memory, association, and affordance — the bakery that smells like a bakery, the corner where the wind always hits, the tree that flowers a week before the others. When you navigate by phone, you get a route. When you navigate by wits, you accumulate places. And places are what the hippocampus is for. The cabbies of London did not merely learn streets; they built a city inside their skulls, and the building changed the shape of the builder. The McGill studies suggest the inverse: that the phone-shape of navigation builds a thinner city, and a thinner map, and perhaps — this is speculation, but it is the kind of speculation worth having — a thinner sense of what it means to be somewhere.

None of this is an argument for smashing your phone. The device in your pocket is a miracle, and it has saved lives and marriages and a great many arguments about which exit to take. But a tool is different from a crutch, and the difference is whether you can put it down. The question is not whether to use GPS but whether you can still, sometimes, choose not to — whether you can leave the house with a destination in mind and no route, and let the city do the rest.

I have started doing this on purpose. Not often, and not ostentatiously — I am not going to pretend I have renounced the blue dot, because I have not, and because a man who renounces the blue dot is insufferable. But once a week or so I walk somewhere I know roughly how to reach and I deliberately don't check. I take the wrong turn. I let the wrong turn stand. I notice the affordances: the gap between buildings that might be a passage, the smell of the bakery, the way the light falls at four o'clock and makes a street I have walked a hundred times look like a street I have never seen. And occasionally — not often, but occasionally — I arrive somewhere I did not intend to go, and it is better than where I was headed. This is not a profound insight. It is roughly the insight of a golden retriever. But it is the kind of insight that a phone will never give you, because a phone has never once been lost, and so a phone has never once been found.

The brain, it turns out, is not a GPS. It is a place-maker. It builds worlds out of attention, and the worlds it builds are only as rich as the attention it pays. Every time we hand the navigation to the machine, we hand over a little of the making. The blue dot is never wrong. But the blue dot is also never *surprised*, and surprise is where the world gets interesting — where the map fails and the place begins.

So: get lost, occasionally, on purpose. Turn the wrong way. Leave the phone in your pocket until you have genuinely, usefully, humiliatingly lost the thread. Stand there for four seconds, feeling the small panic, and then look around. The bakery is that way. The river is that way. The city is bigger than you thought, and it has been waiting, patiently, for you to notice.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished essay, but its recurring metaphors, self-deprecating narrator, and intimate invitation give it a distinctive voice beyond a general public-intellectual argument.

## Grounded reading
The voice is learned but conversational, moving from neuroscience and urban theory into a personal practice without losing its central image of the blue dot. Its pathos is gentle: the essay acknowledges the real convenience and safety of GPS, then mourns the quieter loss of attention and encounter that can accompany outsourcing navigation. The narrator’s admission that getting lost can feel like “a small failure and a small gift” keeps the case for disorientation from becoming a scold. The reader is invited to try a modest experiment—take a wrong turn, look around, and let the city become legible in a different way.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds navigation as a way of attending to and making a place, not merely finding a route. It links GPS use to the atrophy of spatial skill and diminished curiosity, drawing on place cells, London cabbies, Polynesian navigation, flânerie, desire paths, and the narrator’s own walks. Its moral claim is measured rather than anti-technology: tools matter, but being able to put them down preserves the chance to notice, be surprised, and build a richer sense of where one is.

## Evidence line
> The blue dot is never mistaken, and so the world around it becomes wallpaper.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample’s sustained motif of disorientation as a route to attention, reinforced by specific learning and a recognizable self-deprecating narrator, makes this a distinctively revealing piece.
